question: What happened when Italy's law requiring durum-wheat pasta collided with the European single market?
answer: Italy lost at the border and kept the rule at home. A 1967 law let Italian dried pasta be made only from durum semolina. In 1988 the European Court of Justice ruled it could not bar soft-wheat pasta from other member states. Italian factories stayed bound; foreign packets beside theirs did not.
move: A rule that stops at a border can end up binding only the home side.
ask: Is a rule of mine only binding on me, while others slip past it?
reference: Case 407/85, Drei Glocken GmbH and Kritzinger v USL Centro-Sud, European Court of Justice, judgment of 14 July 1988
